content: The systematic reviews conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) were designed to address specific PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions. These reviews were supported by external experts with subject-matter expertise, as well as expertise in systematic reviews and the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. A follow-up meeting of the Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health was held from November 29 to December 2, 2011. During this meeting, WHO presented the systematic reviews of evidence and a draft recommendation that had been prepared prior to the meeting. The draft recommendation included the following components: A summary of the evidence derived from the systematic reviews. Draft GRADE evidence profiles assessing the quality of the body of evidence. Identification of potential research gaps, concerns, and opportunities for feasible implementation of the recommendations in diverse cultural contexts. Appropriate references. The NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health discussed the evidence and the GRADE assessment of the quality of evidence. They provided advice to WHO on the interpretation of the evidence, the scoping of the guideline, evidence appraisal, and decision-making processes. The subgroup also reviewed the draft recommendation and reached a consensus on its content. The systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles for each critical outcome were used to draft the guideline. The strength of each recommendation was classified based on several considerations, including the desirable and undesirable effects of the recommendation, the overall quality of the evidence, values and preferences related to the recommendation in different settings, and the cost of implementation options available to public health authorities in various contexts. This classification was discussed among NUGAG members, invited external resource persons, and members of the WHO Secretariat present at the meeting. The final wording of the recommendations and their strength was based on the consensus of the WHO Secretariat members and NUGAG members present. There were no strong disagreements among the NUGAG members. From February 1 to February 29, 2012, a draft of the guideline was made available for public comment. Participants in the External Expert and Stakeholder Panel were consulted, and other interested parties were invited to provide feedback. Over 165 comments were received from 30 individuals and representatives of stakeholder groups. WHO reviewed these comments and made appropriate updates to the guideline. The finalized guideline was then presented to the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health for finalization during their meeting on March 27–30, 2012. The finalized guideline was submitted for clearance by WHO before publication. In accordance with WHO’s rules, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before participating. The declaration of interest forms for all guideline group members were reviewed by WHO when finalizing the composition of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health. All NUGAG members, external experts, and special invitees participating in each NUGAG meeting submitted a declaration of interests form along with their curriculum vitae. Additionally, each participant verbally declared their interests at the beginning of each meeting. The procedures for managing conflicts of interest strictly adhered to WHO’s guidelines for declaration of interests for WHO experts. The potential interests declared by members of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health, as well as external experts and resource persons, are summarized in Annex 9. This guideline is based on a review of the epidemiologic literature, including three new systematic reviews conducted by WHO. One of these reviews included a reanalysis of data from a fourth systematic review to explore data needed for the evidence base for this guideline. Specific health outcomes considered in adults included blood pressure, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, stroke, coronary heart disease, renal function, blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and other potential adverse effects. In children, the outcomes considered included blood pressure, blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and other potential adverse effects. The specific research questions guiding these systematic reviews were: What is the effect of decreased sodium intake compared with higher sodium intake on health outcomes in adults and children? Is a sodium intake of less than 2 grams per day associated with greater health benefits compared to an intake of more than 2 grams per day? Evidence was considered conclusive of either a benefit or harm from decreased sodium intake if the point estimate suggested a benefit or harm and the 95% confidence interval (CI) did not overlap a threshold of relevance. If the real value (e.g., the high or low 95% CI value) was still of clinical relevance, the evidence was considered conclusive. Conversely, if the real value was not of clinical relevance, the evidence was considered inconclusive. In such cases, point estimates were considered either precise or imprecise depending on the clinical relevance of the confidence interval. Blood Pressure in Adults A systematic review exploring the relationship between sodium intake and blood pressure, as well as potential adverse effects, identified 37 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reporting on systolic or diastolic blood pressure, renal function, blood lipid concentrations, or plasma/urinary catecholamine levels. These studies were conducted in Australia, Europe, North America, and New Zealand, covering a variety of countries, climates, and cultural contexts. Twenty-four studies were conducted in individuals with hypertension (defined as blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg), five in individuals without hypertension, and eight in mixed populations. No studies reported results for women separately from men; two studies were conducted in men, and 35 studies included mixed-gender populations. All studies measured 24-hour urinary sodium excretion to estimate sodium intake, assuming equivalence between intake and excretion. The studies had a duration of four weeks or more. The results consistently showed a decrease in blood pressure with reduced sodium intake in adults, consistent with findings from five previous systematic reviews. WHO conducted a meta-analysis of data addressing whether sodium consumption of less than 2 grams per day is more beneficial than consumption of more than 2 grams per day. Two studies with three comparisons randomly assigned participants to multiple intervention arms with varying levels of sodium intake. One arm consumed reduced sodium at a level of less than 2 grams per day, another consumed reduced sodium but more than 2 grams per day, and a third consumed higher sodium levels. The results showed a significant reduction in blood pressure with sodium intake below 2 grams per day. Cardiovascular Outcomes in Adults WHO conducted a systematic review of epidemiological evidence on the relationship between sodium intake and all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and coronary heart disease. Two recent systematic reviews were identified, one including RCTs and the other cohort studies. Data from the RCT review were re-analyzed to exclude a study in an acutely ill population. The authors concluded that there was insufficient power to detect a statistically significant effect due to the limited number of events, even after synthesizing the data. Blood Pressure in Children WHO conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials to assess the effect of reduced sodium intake on blood pressure in children aged 2–15 years. Nine controlled trials and one cohort study were included. The controlled trials involved children aged 5–15 years, while the cohort study followed children aged 5–17 years for seven years. The results showed a reduction in blood pressure with reduced sodium intake, consistent with findings in adults. Renal Function and Blood Lipids The systematic review also addressed potential adverse effects of reduced sodium intake, including changes in blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and renal function. Fifteen studies reported on blood lipid concentrations, and five studies reported on indicators of renal function. The results showed little or no adverse effects of reduced sodium intake on blood lipids and suggested a potential beneficial effect on renal function. In conclusion, the evidence supports the recommendation to reduce sodium intake to less than 2 grams per day in adults and children to improve health outcomes, particularly by lowering blood pressure and reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease.
